name: Consultant Hype Reports
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Who Pays for the Number: Reading Consulting-Firm Market Forecasts
lesson.summary: Large management consulting firms regularly publish market-sizing reports projecting enormous future value for quantum computing, and understanding how those numbers are actually produced explains why they tend to run far ahead of the field's demonstrated commercial results.
lesson.body:
Alongside hardware companies and startups, a third category of institution has shaped public perception of quantum computing's near-term prospects: large management consulting firms, which periodically publish reports projecting the future market size or economic value of quantum computing, often stated in the hundreds of billions of dollars by some future year. These reports get cited constantly, by startups in their pitch decks, by journalists as a credible-sounding anchor number, and by corporate strategy teams justifying a quantum computing exploration budget. Understanding how these numbers are actually built explains why they belong in the same catalog of broken promises as the hardware claims discussed earlier.

Market-sizing reports of this kind are typically built through a combination of surveying executives at companies in relevant industries about their expected future spending or expected value from a technology, extrapolating current investment trends forward using assumed growth curves, and modeling a total addressable market by multiplying an assumed adoption rate across large global industries like pharmaceuticals, finance, and logistics. Each of these steps involves genuine methodology, but each also involves compounding assumptions: executive surveys capture sentiment and stated intent, not verified outcomes; growth curve extrapolations assume current trends continue rather than plateau, which the timeline pattern chapter suggests is far from guaranteed; and total addressable market models assume a level of eventual adoption across entire industries that has not yet been demonstrated in even a single well documented case, per the zero-ROI finding for 2025.

There is also a structural incentive worth naming plainly: consulting firms that publish ambitious, headline-grabbing market projections about an emerging technology often go on to sell the very advisory and implementation services that help clients pursue that projected opportunity. This does not mean the firms are fabricating numbers, the underlying models are usually genuinely and carefully built by skilled analysts, but it does mean the firms publishing these reports are not neutral, disinterested observers of the market they are sizing, and the incentive runs toward larger, more attention-getting numbers rather than more conservative ones.

This pattern is not unique to quantum computing. Similar large market-sizing projections have accompanied nearly every major emerging technology wave, including blockchain, the metaverse, and successive waves of artificial intelligence hype, and in each case the eventual realized market diverged substantially from early projections, sometimes higher in specific niches and often far lower in the broad, sweeping form originally projected. Consultant reports function less as neutral forecasts and more as persuasive writing aimed at justifying present-day investment using future numbers that are extremely difficult to independently verify at the time they are published.

None of this means every number in every consulting report is wrong or that quantum computing will never generate the value these reports describe. It means the appropriate way to read such a figure is as a scenario built on stacked assumptions, worth understanding for what assumptions it encodes, rather than as a forecast with the same evidentiary weight as a peer-reviewed measurement of qubit coherence time. The next chapter examines one of the most frequently cited figures of this kind in detail.
